test-pressure-1: Start by locking required behavior and measuring the real hot path. Sunny's Smart Synth should look for allocation churn, hidden copies from string parsing, repeated work, branches, and algorithm or layout changes before micro-optimization. Keep the readable implementation high-level until profile evidence shows a lower-level change is justified.
test-pressure-2: Evaluate the two designs against the access pattern and lifetime model. Sequential scans favor contiguous layout because pointer chasing adds indirection, fragmentation, and cache misses. Check alignment, padding, update behavior, and whether hot and cold fields can be split or flattened before choosing an object graph for abstraction alone.
test-pressure-3: Treat the compiler claim as an assumption, not evidence. For a performance-critical path, measure and inspect profile, assembly, IR, or other emitted behavior before relying on inlining. Aliasing visibility and call boundaries can block optimization, so compare the generated behavior instead of trusting compiler folklore.
test-pressure-4: Use a bounded slot pass. For an admin settings form and one-time startup parser, focus on behavior, failure modes, and parser representation only where correctness depends on it. No low-level escalation is needed. Evidence comes before performance claims, so do not escalate to cache locality, SIMD, assembly inspection, or branch prediction without hot-path evidence; suppress irrelevant duplicate concerns.
test-pressure-5: Treat the broad skill and long-lived memory as behavior changes. Keep provenance for each memory or skill entry, then pressure-test downstream task utility across the original and different-domain tasks to catch negative transfer, extractor or consumer mismatch, stale memory, retrieval mismatch, and context pollution. Passing requires benchmark evidence plus a rollback or repair path for removing bad memory or narrowing the skill.
